newsitem.title: USA: NYC needs to close out-year gaps - state monitor.
newsitem.headline: NYC needs to close out-year gaps - state monitor.

text.p: New York City needs to make more of an effort to close huge, looming budget gaps, the New York State Control Board said on Thursday, specifically citing how the Giuliani Administration will use this year's surplus.

The state control board's latest report was issued on Thursday, but was partly out of date because New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani late Wednesday reached a preliminary pact on a new budget with the City Council Speaker.

The Democrat-led City Council was expected to begin voting on the $33.4 billion budget plan early Thursday evening, and due to the strong leadership by Speaker Peter Vallone, its approval largely was considered a given.
As a result of the pending fiscal year 1998 budget pact, the most useful part of the state board's analysis concerned the 1997 fiscal year that ends on June 30.
"Basically, it's a document of record for what happened in 1997," said Jeffrey Sommer, a spokesman for the board.

The report said, "We commend the city for commiting a portion of its fiscal year 1997 surplus to reduce projected budget gaps in both fiscal years 1998 and 1999 rather than consuming the entire roll in fiscal year 1998."
It continued, "However, it should be noted that the city has an opportunity to use these non-recurring resources in a way that provides recurring budget relief beyond fiscal year 1999."
By fiscal 2001, the city faces nearly a $3 billion budget gap, though it has balanced its books for each of the past 17 years.

The city in fiscal 1997 replaced $607 million of funds that had been reserved for pay-as-you-go capital financing with general obligation bond sales. The decision was made because the Giuliani Administration lost a court fight to sell its water system, the report said.
New York City could have used all or part of its fiscal 1997 surplus for an equal amount of the proceeds it raised from selling general obligation bonds.

Giuliani has projected the city will end the present fiscal year with $1.3 billion of extra revenues, which will be used to help create a $500 million general reserve, and prepay debt service in fiscal 1998 and fiscal 1998.

"Paying for debt one year early does not reduce debt service, nor limit its growth in future years," the state control board said, adding that had Giuliani paid for part of the capital program with the operating budget, this would have reduced future debt levels and debt service.
